title: The Pigeons That Invented Superstition 🐦🔮
yt_description:
In 1948, B. F. Skinner gave eight hungry pigeons food every 15 seconds, no matter what they did. Six of the eight developed rituals: one turned counter-clockwise two or three times between meals, another kept thrusting its head into an upper corner of the box, a third tossed its head as if lifting an invisible bar. Skinner published it as "'Superstition' in the Pigeon" (Journal of Experimental Psychology, 1948). Later researchers, like Staddon and Simmelhag (1971), debated the explanation, but the behavior was real.
The lesson: when good things happen by chance, we credit whatever we were doing.

script: In 1948, psychologist B. F. Skinner put eight hungry pigeons into eight boxes. Every fifteen seconds, a little food appeared. No matter what the pigeon did. There was nothing to learn. The food came by the clock. But the pigeons didn't know that. Whatever a bird happened to be doing when the food arrived, it did again. And again. One pigeon started turning in circles, counter-clockwise. Two or three turns between every meal. Another kept pushing its head into one top corner of the box. A third tossed its head up, as if lifting an invisible bar. Six of the eight birds built a ritual. Each one acted as if its dance made the food come. Skinner titled his paper: superstition in the pigeon. Later scientists argued about why it happens. But the rituals were real. This is called the ritual trap. Psychologists call it superstitious conditioning. When something good happens by chance, we credit whatever we were doing at that moment. The lucky socks. The right way to throw the dice. The trader who only buys on Tuesdays. Our brains hate randomness. So we invent a cause, and then we obey it. Before you repeat a ritual, ask yourself: is it working, or is the food just coming by the clock?
